text: Supervised learning shows a model examples paired with a correct answer, a label, and the model learns to predict that answer for new cases. Someone has to assign those labels in the first place, and the model trusts them as ground truth, wrong or biased, it inherits exactly that.

Labeling is usually where the most direct human judgment happens in building a training dataset. Two labelers can reasonably disagree about whether a comment is toxic or a transaction looks fraudulent, and whichever judgment gets recorded becomes, as far as the model is concerned, objective truth. That connects directly to last lesson's label bias, a labeler's own inconsistency becomes part of what the model learns to reproduce.

Four governance concerns matter specifically here. Inter-rater agreement, how often multiple labelers agree, low agreement signals an ambiguous task or unclear instructions. Labeling instructions as a governed artifact, they function like a policy document, and changing them partway through without documenting it can silently split a dataset into inconsistent halves. Who's doing the labeling, in-house, contracted, or crowdsourced each raise different training and data-handling questions. Label provenance, which labeler or process produced which label, under which version of the instructions.

A governed organization doesn't just ask whether data was labeled, it asks whether the instructions are documented, whether agreement between labelers was ever measured, and whether anyone can trace a label back to who produced it. Absent all three, a labeled dataset is really an unverified one.
That closes the governance of the data itself. Next up: synthetic data, which raises a different set of questions entirely.
